newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Populist vows to fight Swiss gold foundation.
newsitem.headline: Populist vows to fight Swiss gold foundation.

text.p: Swiss populist Christoph Blocher vowed on Tuesday to lead a voter uprising against the government's bold plans to create a huge humanitarian foundation by selling off part of the country's official gold reserves.

Accusing the cabinet of bowing to extortion by Switzerland's fiercest critics, Blocher told parliament in Berne he would do his best to ensure Swiss voters overturn the plan when it comes up in a referendum next year.

Most other parties back the planned seven billion Swiss franc ($4.8 billion) foundation as a concrete expression of gratitude that the Swiss escaped two devastating world wars and of solidarity with victims of poverty, human rights abuses and the Holocaust.
Initial opinion polls also show most Swiss back the idea, unveiled by Swiss President Arnold Koller earlier this month.

But Blocher, from the right-wing Swiss People's Party, told a debate over Switzerland's role as a World War Two financial centre the foundation was a thinly disguised bid to buy off critics of Switzerland's wartime commercial links to the Nazis.

"We have nothing to apologise for over this policy and we have nothing to pay. Whether you want it to be or not, a payment is an admission of guilt," he declared, arguing that doing business with the Nazis helped ensure Switzerland's survival.

He said modern-day banks and private businesses were well within their rights in helping finance a Holocaust memorial fund amid a global outcry over allegations Swiss banks hoarded billions of dollars in dormant wealth from Holocaust victims.

But he added Berne was going too far by proposing to sell off public gold reserves to create the Swiss Solidarity Foundation, which would pay out hundreds of millions of francs a year to deserving people in Switzerland and abroad.
"This foundation must not be created," insisted Blocher, the man whose isolationist arguments helped persuade Swiss voters in 1992 to reject closer ties with the European Union.

"They could blackmail banks, you can blackmail governments, you can blackmail national banks, you can force them to give in. (But) I would like to see if they can blackmail an entire people at the ballot box. They have to get through the eye of this needle, and I will do my utmost that we do not yield."

He did not say who "they" were, and made no mention of Jewish groups who were outraged when outgoing Swiss President Jean-Pascal Delamuraz accused them last year of "extortion and blackmail" for demanding Berne compensate Holocaust victims.

Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger acknowledged the surprise proposal to set up the foundation was prompted by the current debate about Switzerland's past, but insisted that move reflected a sovereign decision by the cabinet in Berne.

"It is a work of solidarity that Switzerland would itself create on the 150th anniversary of its birth as a federal state," he said, "without outside pressure, independent of historical aspects and conscious of how important a humanitarian tradition and solidarity are for our country's identity."
Just as a generation of Swiss stood up against Hitler when they were surrounded by fascists, today's Swiss have to stand up against a misguided give-away of public property, he said.
"The issue here as well is resistance or confrontation... I am for resistance that will show the world that a small country too can command respect," Blocher said.

Other speakers tended to support the foundation as a bold stroke that could inspire the Swiss to make constructive contibutions to the future by carefully considering the past. ($ = 1.459 Swiss Francs)
